_note: INFORMATION TEXTS for the English literacy year (Daily Teaching System, Part 12.3; read by a US Grade 1 reading reviewer 2026-11-15 and corrected by every finding; read a second time after the corrections (four small wording points, applied)). The reading banks held stories only; the Common Core RI standards need texts that inform. Grade 1: about 60 to 75 words in two sections, each with a heading; two words in bold; a three-word glossary; one library picture with a caption. Every fact must be one a teacher can confirm; every question has one right answer that a sentence of the text gives (its 1-based number is `sentence`). `topic` = the main topic and two wrong choices (a detail of the text; a thing the text only mentions). `full` = the whole answer sentence of a question (it starts with `starter`); `lure` = a word of the text that is not in bold (a wrong choice of the bold-word question); `capChoices` = two wrong answers of the caption question; `picture2` = a second picture of something the text tells about, with a sample caption. `features` = find-it questions answered from a text feature, not from the running text. `headLure` = a heading the text does not have (the third choice of a heading question: a child may call the title the main heading). KINDERGARTEN (`k`; read by a US kindergarten reviewer 2026-11-15 and corrected by every finding, then read a second time and corrected again): four sentences in big print; every question is read aloud by the teacher and answered by circling one of three library pictures (`right`, `wrong`; `draw` = the question as it stands on the levels where the child draws); `topic` = the picture of the main topic and the pictures of the two key details; `details` = the numbers of the two sentences that are key details. Added 2026-11-15 for two more pages and read by a US kindergarten reviewer (every finding applied): the texts `oak-trees` and `rain` (`since`: the two first pages do not draw them, so their published pages stay what they are); `match` = the matching page of a text: the picture of each sentence, its own wording of a sentence where needed, and which pictures may be the missing one on the hard level; `change` = what comes first and what comes then in a text that tells a change, a picture that is no part of it, the two words, and its own wording of the text where needed. GRADE 2 (`g2`; read twice by a US Grade 2 reviewer 2026-11-15 and corrected by every finding): about 150 words in three parts (the pages 1-3 of a small book), each with a heading and one bold word; two pictures with captions; a four-word glossary; an index (word → page); `focus` = what each part is mostly about, `focusLure` = a focus no part has; `topic` = the main topic, a detail and a too-wide choice; `features` = six find-it questions (a caption question names its two wrong answers; the others take them from the text). GRADE 2 DIAGRAM TEXTS (`g2d`) and HOW-IT-IS-MADE TEXTS (`g2s`), written 2026-11-16, read by a US Grade 2 reviewer and corrected by every finding: a `g2d` text has two paragraphs (about 115 words; it never says how many stages there are) and a cycle diagram of four or five drawn stages with labels and arrows (the text names only the labels in `textNames`; the hardest level leaves out the label of the stage `blank` and the arrow that starts from the stage `gap`, which is next to it and never the arrow back to the first stage); a `g2s` text has an opening paragraph and four steps that begin with First, Next, Then and Finally (about 135 words), three library pictures, the four steps as short statements, three questions to circle (the signal word of a step named by what it tells, a detail, and why one step comes before another) and the same why-question to write. (2026-11-16: three captions of the `g2` texts elephants and spiders were rewritten to tell about their picture, a finding of the reviewer who read the renders.) A `g2d` text also holds `facts` for the page Text or Diagram?: three facts only the text tells and three only the diagram tells (a name or an order, or, marked `picture`, something the drawing shows). A `g2s` text also holds `clauses`: its four steps as short clauses for the sentences of the page Before and After. KINDERGARTEN PAIRS (`k2`), written 2026-11-16: two fact texts of four short sentences on one topic; two library pictures of things BOTH texts tell about, two of the first text only, two of the second only (each with the `word` that stands in the text and a `label` a child can write). GRADE 3 TEXTS (`g3`), 2026-11-16: about 230 words in FOUR paragraphs, each with a heading and a `focus` (what it is mostly about; `focusLure` fits none), one library picture; the main idea as a sentence with one that is too narrow and one that is too wide, three key details and one sentence that is not in the text, a summary; five questions, each with the paragraph that proves the answer and the proving sentence word for word; four sentences of the text with the question each answers and a wrong question about the same paragraph (`lure`). READ 2026-11-16 by a US Grade 3 reviewer with the rendered pages; every finding applied.

g2d.title: How a Butterfly Grows
paras: A butterfly does not look the same all its life.
It changes as it grows.
The diagram shows its stages in order.
Follow the arrows to see what comes next.
A butterfly begins its life inside a tiny egg.
The young animal that comes out of it is very hungry.
It eats leaves day after day and grows fast.
Then it hangs from a stem or a leaf.
It sheds its skin one last time, and a hard case forms around its body.
Inside the case, its body slowly changes.
At last the case splits open, and a butterfly climbs out.
Its wings are wet and soft at first.
When they are dry, the butterfly flies away.
Later, a grown female butterfly lays tiny eggs on a leaf.

The plant uses sunlight, air, and water to make its own food.
It grows taller and gets more leaves.

One half of the moon is always lit by the sun.
As the moon travels around Earth, we see more or less of that bright half.
Sometimes we see all of it.
The moon looks like a bright circle, and we call it the full moon.
Sometimes the bright half faces away from us, and we can hardly see the moon at all.
The phases repeat about once a month.

g2s.title: From Flower to Honey Jar
paras: Honey is made by honeybees.
It takes many bees and many days to fill one jar.
First, bees fly from flower to flower.
They suck up a sweet juice called nectar and carry it back to the hive.
Next, the bees pass the nectar from mouth to mouth, and it starts to change.
They put it into the small wax cells of the honeycomb and fan it with their wings.
The moving air dries the nectar until it is thick and sticky.
Now it is honey, and the bees close each full cell with a lid of wax.
Then, a beekeeper lifts the honeycomb out of the hive.
The beekeeper cuts off the wax lids and spins the honeycomb in a machine, so the honey flows out.
Enough honey stays in the hive for the bees to eat in winter.
Finally, the honey is poured into jars.
It is ready to eat.

g2s.title: How Bread Is Made
paras: This bread is made from flour, water, salt, and yeast.
Yeast is a tiny living thing that makes bread soft and light.
A baker makes it in four main steps.
First, the baker mixes everything in a big bowl and kneads it.
Kneading means pressing and folding the dough again and again until it is smooth.
Next, the dough rests in a warm place.
The yeast makes tiny bubbles of gas, so the dough slowly rises.
After an hour or more, it is about twice as big.
Then, the baker shapes the dough into a loaf, lets it rise a little more, and puts it into a hot oven.
The heat bakes the dough and turns the crust brown.
Finally, the baker takes the bread out of the oven and lets it cool.
Now it can be sliced and eaten.

g2s.title: From Tree to Paper
paras: Most paper is made from wood.
A paper mill turns logs into paper in four big steps.
First, trees are cut down, and trucks bring the logs to the mill.
Many of the trees are pines.
A machine takes off the bark and cuts the logs into small chips.
Next, the chips are cooked in a big tank.
They fall apart into a soft, wet mush called pulp.
Then, the pulp is sprayed onto a wide moving screen.
Water drips out through the screen, and the tiny bits of wood stick together in a thin sheet.
Finally, heavy rollers press the sheet, and hot rollers dry it.
The dry paper is wound into giant rolls.
Later it is cut into sheets for books and notebooks.
Used paper can be turned into pulp again.
That is why it is good to recycle paper.

g2s.title: From Sheep to Sweater
paras: A wool sweater begins on a sheep.
It takes four steps to turn the wool into a sweater.
First, a farmer cuts off the sheep's thick wool in spring.
This is called shearing.
It does not hurt the sheep.
The wool grows back, the way your hair does after a haircut.
Next, the wool is washed, because it is full of dirt and grease.
The clean wool is combed until it is soft and smooth.
Then, the wool is spun.
That means pulling and twisting it into a long, strong thread called yarn.
The yarn can be dyed red, blue, or any other color.
Finally, the yarn is knitted into a sweater.
Wool holds in heat, so the sweater keeps you warm on cold days.

g2s.title: From Orange Tree to Juice Glass
paras: Orange juice starts in a grove of orange trees.
It takes four steps to get the juice from the tree to your glass.
First, workers pick the oranges when they are ripe.
Trucks carry the fruit to a juice plant.
There a machine scrubs every orange clean, so no dirt from the peels gets into the juice.
Next, machines squeeze the juice out of the oranges.
The peels and the seeds are taken away.
One glass of juice takes about three oranges.
Then, the juice is heated for a short time.
The heat kills germs that could make people sick.
Right after that, the juice is cooled again.
Finally, the juice is poured into cartons and bottles.
Cold trucks take them to stores, and the juice stays cold until someone buys it.

g3.title: Lighthouses

parts.heading: Keeping Ships Safe
parts.focus: why lighthouses were built
sentences: For hundreds of years, sailing at night was dangerous.
Ships could hit rocks or run onto sand that the sailors could not see.
To keep ships safe, people built tall towers with a bright light on top.
These towers are called lighthouses.
They stand on coasts and islands, where the water is most dangerous.

parts.heading: How the Light Works
parts.focus: how the light of a lighthouse works
sentences: The light of a lighthouse has to be seen from far away.
Long ago, keepers burned wood or coal on top of the tower.
Later they used oil lamps.
In the 1820s, a French scientist named Augustin Fresnel invented a special lens.
Its rings of glass bend the light of one lamp into a strong beam.
Sailors can see the beam from about 20 miles away.

parts.heading: The Lighthouse Keeper
parts.focus: the work of a lighthouse keeper
sentences: Most lighthouses once had a keeper who lived there, often with a family.
The keeper lit the lamp at sunset and put it out at sunrise.
During the night, the keeper made sure the light never went out.
The lens had to be cleaned every day.
In fog, the keeper also sounded a loud horn or bell, because ships could not see the light.

parts.heading: Lighthouses Today
parts.focus: what lighthouses are like today
sentences: Today, electric lamps turn on and off by themselves, so lighthouses no longer need keepers.
Ships also find their way with the help of satellites.
Still, many lighthouses keep shining as a backup.
Each one flashes in its own pattern, so sailors can tell which lighthouse they see.
Some old lighthouses have become museums that people can visit.

g3.title: Living on the Space Station

parts.heading: A Laboratory Above Earth
parts.focus: what the space station is and who lives there
sentences: The International Space Station is a laboratory that circles Earth about 250 miles above the ground.
It travels very fast and goes around Earth about 16 times every day.
Astronauts from many countries live and work there, usually for about six months at a time.
The first crew arrived in the year 2000, and people have lived on the station ever since.

parts.heading: Floating All Day
parts.focus: how everything floats on the station
sentences: On the station, everything floats, and so do the astronauts.
They do not walk.
They push off a wall and glide to where they want to go.
Tools, pencils, and even drops of water float away if nobody holds them.
That is why the walls are covered with straps and strips of Velcro that keep things in place.

parts.heading: Eating and Sleeping
parts.focus: how astronauts eat and sleep
sentences: Meals come in sealed bags and cans, so crumbs and drops cannot drift into the machines.
Astronauts drink through straws from closed pouches.
At night, each astronaut zips into a sleeping bag that is tied to the wall of a small cabin.
Without the ties, a sleeping astronaut would slowly float around the station.

parts.heading: Work and Exercise
parts.focus: what astronauts do during the day
sentences: Astronauts spend most of the day on science experiments and on repairs.
They also exercise about two hours every day.
In space, muscles and bones do not have to carry the weight of the body, so they get weak.
Running on a treadmill and pulling against machines keeps the astronauts strong for their return to Earth.

g3.title: Emperor Penguins

parts.heading: The Coldest Home on Earth
parts.focus: how cold the home of the emperor penguins is
sentences: Emperor penguins live in Antarctica, the coldest place on Earth.
In winter the temperature can drop to 40 degrees below zero, and icy winds blow across the ice.
Emperor penguins are the largest penguins.
A grown one stands almost four feet tall.
Thick fat and tightly packed feathers keep its body warm.

parts.heading: One Egg in Winter
parts.focus: how the father takes care of the egg
sentences: Most birds lay their eggs in spring, but emperor penguins lay theirs at the start of winter.
The mother lays one egg and passes it to the father.
Then she walks many miles to the sea to hunt for fish.
The father balances the egg on his feet and covers it with a warm fold of skin.
For about two months, while he keeps the egg, he eats nothing at all.

parts.heading: Huddling Together
parts.focus: how the fathers stay warm together
sentences: To get through the storms, the fathers stand close together in a big group called a huddle.
Thousands of penguins press against each other.
The birds in the middle are warm, and the birds on the outside are cold.
So the penguins keep changing places.
Every bird gets a turn in the warm middle.

parts.heading: The Chick Arrives
parts.focus: how the parents raise the chick
sentences: When the chick hatches, the mother comes back with food in her stomach.
Now the hungry father can go to the sea.
For the next months, the parents take turns feeding the chick.
By summer, the young penguin has grown waterproof feathers.
Then it is ready to swim and to catch its own fish.

g3.title: The Pony Express

parts.heading: Mail for the West
parts.focus: why the Pony Express was started
sentences: In 1860, sending a letter across the United States took a long time.
Mail to California traveled by stagecoach or by ship, and it could take three weeks or more to arrive.
Three businessmen had a new idea.
Fast riders on fast horses would carry the mail.
They called their new mail service the Pony Express.

parts.heading: From Station to Station
parts.focus: how the mail moved along the route
sentences: The route ran almost 2,000 miles, from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California.
A rider galloped about ten miles to the next station.
There he jumped onto a fresh horse and raced on.
After about 75 miles, a new rider took over the bag of mail.
Day and night, the mail kept moving.

parts.heading: Brave Young Riders
parts.focus: what the riders and their work were like
sentences: The riders were young and light, so the horses could run fast.
Many were teenagers.
They rode through deserts, over mountains, and across rivers, in summer heat and in winter snow.
The work was hard and dangerous, but the mail almost always got through.
A letter now crossed the country in about ten days.

parts.heading: The End of the Pony Express
parts.focus: why the Pony Express ended
sentences: The Pony Express lasted only about 18 months.
In October 1861, workers finished a telegraph line that reached all the way to California.
Now a message could be sent across the country in minutes over a wire.
Nobody needed the fast riders anymore.
The Pony Express closed, but people still tell its story today.

g3.title: Blue Whales

parts.heading: The Biggest Animal
parts.focus: how big a blue whale is
sentences: The blue whale is the largest animal that has ever lived.
It can grow up to 100 feet long, about as long as three school buses.
Its tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant.
A blue whale is heavier than any dinosaur we know.
Blue whales swim in oceans all around the world.

parts.heading: Tiny Food for a Giant
parts.focus: what a blue whale eats and how it catches its food
sentences: This giant eats some of the smallest animals in the sea.
Its food is krill, which look like shrimp and are about as long as your finger.
A blue whale has no teeth.
Instead, long plates called baleen hang from its upper jaw like a comb.
The whale takes a huge mouthful of water, pushes the water out, and the krill stay behind.

parts.heading: Breathing Air
parts.focus: how a blue whale breathes
sentences: A blue whale lives in the water, but it is not a fish.
It is a mammal, and it breathes air just as you do.
It has to come to the surface to breathe.
There it blows out through two blowholes on top of its head, and the spray can shoot 30 feet into the air.
Then the whale breathes in and dives again.

parts.heading: Mothers and Calves
parts.focus: how a calf grows up
sentences: A baby whale is called a calf.
At birth it is already about 25 feet long.
The calf drinks milk from its mother and gains about 200 pounds every day.
Mother and calf stay together for about half a year.
After that, the young whale finds its own krill.
